WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 2: screening: systematic screening for tuberculosis disease
abstract:
Tuberculosis remains one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent despite being largely preventable and curable. This updated WHO guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on systematic screening for tuberculosis disease to support earlier diagnosis, timely initiation of treatment and reduced transmission. It revises the 2013 guidance in light of new evidence on the effectiveness of screening interventions and the performance of screening tools, using the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence and the strength of recommendations. The document is intended to assist countries in planning and implementing screening strategies adapted to their epidemiological and health system contexts.

The guideline presents recommendations for systematic screening in the general population and in groups at increased risk of tuberculosis, including people living with HIV, household contacts, prisoners, miners, migrants and other vulnerable populations. It also reviews the use of symptom screening, chest radiography, computer-aided detection software, C-reactive protein and molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests as screening tools, together with guidance on monitoring, evaluation and implementation considerations. The publication identifies research gaps and is accompanied by an operational handbook providing practical guidance for applying the recommendations in national tuberculosis programmes.

title: WHO guideline for screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions for cervical cancer prevention
abstract:
This second edition of the WHO guideline provides updated evidence-based recommendations for screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions to prevent cervical cancer in both the general population of women and women living with HIV. Developed in support of the WHO global strategy to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem, the guideline responds to advances in screening technologies and implementation approaches by updating previous recommendations and introducing new guidance to simplify clinical algorithms while improving feasibility, acceptability and programme performance across diverse health system settings. The recommendations were developed in accordance with WHO guideline development procedures using systematic reviews, mathematical modelling where necessary, GRADE assessments of the certainty of evidence, evidence-to-decision frameworks, and consideration of feasibility, costs, acceptability and users’ values and preferences.

The guideline presents recommendations and good practice statements on primary screening tests, screening intervals, age at initiation and cessation of screening, triage strategies, follow-up after positive screening results, treatment approaches, and programme implementation for both population groups. It addresses service delivery, integration with HIV care, implementation considerations, research gaps and dissemination, while emphasizing the transition to HPV DNA testing, the use of evidence-based screening and treatment algorithms, and country adaptation according to available resources and local context to improve coverage, quality of care and cervical cancer prevention.

title: Consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis and STI prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care for key populations
abstract:
This guideline provides consolidated, evidence-based recommendations for the prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care of HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among key populations. It responds to the disproportionate burden of these infections in groups such as men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, people in prisons and other closed settings, and trans and gender diverse individuals, and to the structural barriers that limit their access to health services. The document aims to support countries in strengthening integrated, people-centred responses to these interconnected epidemics.

Developed using WHO guideline standards and the GRADE methodology, the publication brings together existing and new recommendations and organizes them into comprehensive packages of interventions. It addresses enabling factors such as legal and policy environments, stigma, discrimination, violence and community empowerment, alongside essential health interventions including prevention, testing, treatment and harm reduction. The guideline also outlines service delivery approaches, such as community-led services, integration and decentralization, and provides guidance for programme planning, implementation and monitoring. Intended for policy-makers, programme managers and health-care providers, it supports the prioritization of effective, context-appropriate strategies to improve access, coverage and health outcomes for key populations.

title: Consolidated guidelines on person-centred HIV strategic information: strengthening routine data for impact
abstract:
These consolidated guidelines provide normative guidance for strengthening HIV strategic information through person-centred routine data systems that support both clinical care and programme management. Developed in response to persistent gaps in HIV prevention, testing, treatment and retention despite substantial progress in the global HIV response, the guidelines promote the collection and use of individual-level longitudinal data to improve continuity of care, strengthen linkage across services and enhance monitoring of programme performance. They consolidate and update previous WHO guidance while introducing recommendations on person-centred monitoring, digital health information systems, interoperability, data quality, surveillance and the integration of HIV services with tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections and other related conditions.

The publication outlines recommendations and operational guidance on HIV prevention monitoring, patient monitoring, surveillance, digital health data, routine data use, priority indicators and implementation considerations. It emphasizes the transition from aggregate reporting to person-centred, digital information systems that support clinical decision-making, programme improvement and public health action while ensuring data privacy, confidentiality and security. The guidelines also describe minimum datasets, standardized monitoring tools and approaches to improving data quality and using routine information to strengthen service delivery and measure progress towards global HIV targets.

title: Differentiated and simplified pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV prevention: update to WHO implementation guidance: technical brief
Guidelines for diagnosing, preventing and managing cryptococcal disease among adults, adolescents and children living with HIV
abstract:
This guideline provides updated, evidence-informed recommendations for diagnosing, preventing and managing cryptococcal disease among adults, adolescents and children living with HIV. Developed in accordance with WHO Guideline Review Committee procedures, it replaces the 2018 guidance and incorporates important new evidence published in 2021 on the preferred antifungal induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis. The recommendations are based on systematic reviews using the GRADE approach and are supported by considerations of acceptability, values and preferences, feasibility and cost–effectiveness. The document addresses cryptococcal disease as a major opportunistic infection contributing substantially to HIV-related illness, disability and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, and identifies priority knowledge gaps to inform future research.

The guideline recommends updated approaches to the diagnosis, prevention and treatment of cryptococcal disease, including revised guidance on induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis, while maintaining earlier recommendations where evidence remains unchanged. It also outlines principles for implementation within a public health approach and is intended to support HIV programme managers, policy-makers, health-care professionals and people living with HIV in improving the prevention, early diagnosis and clinical management of cryptococcal disease.

title: Guidelines on long-acting injectable cabotegravir for HIV prevention
abstract:
This guideline provides evidence-informed recommendations on the use of long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention in people at substantial risk of HIV infection. Developed according to WHO guideline development procedures, it is based on systematic reviews, GRADE assessments and additional evidence on effectiveness, safety, acceptability, feasibility, equity and cost–effectiveness. The document reviews the global HIV prevention context, the rationale for expanding HIV prevention choices, and the evidence supporting CAB-LA as an additional PrEP option. It also outlines the principles guiding implementation within a public health and human rights framework and identifies the intended audiences for the recommendations.

The guideline recommends that long-acting injectable cabotegravir may be offered as an additional HIV prevention choice as part of combination prevention approaches for people at substantial risk of HIV infection. It discusses key implementation considerations, including HIV testing, service delivery models, comprehensive prevention services, community engagement, provider training and adherence support. The publication also identifies priority research gaps related to safety, drug resistance, delivery strategies and population-level impact, and describes the guideline development process, dissemination strategy and supporting evidence underpinning the recommendation.

title: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 5: management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents
abstract:
Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality among children and adolescents, with substantial gaps in case detection, diagnosis and access to preventive treatment worldwide. This guideline consolidates new and existing WHO recommendations for the management of TB in these populations, replacing the 2014 guidance and reflecting the latest evidence on prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment and models of care. It aims to support countries in strengthening the continuum of TB care and improving health outcomes through evidence-based policies and practices tailored to the specific needs of children, adolescents and their families.

The publication provides recommendations on TB screening and contact investigation, TB preventive treatment, diagnostic approaches, treatment of drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB, management of TB meningitis, and decentralized, family-centred models of care. It incorporates updated evidence on the use of Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, integrated treatment decision algorithms, shortened treatment regimens for non-severe TB, and therapeutic options for multidrug- or rifampicin-resistant disease in children. Developed according to WHO guideline development standards, the document is intended for national TB programmes, policy-makers, health professionals and implementing partners, and contributes to global efforts to reduce TB-related morbidity and mortality in line with the End TB Strategy and Sustainable Development Goals.

title: WHO implementation tool for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV infection: module 13: integrating STI services
abstract:
This module of the WHO Implementation Tool for Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV Infection provides operational guidance on integrating sexually transmitted infection (STI) services into HIV PrEP programmes. Developed for programme managers, decision-makers, facility managers and health-care workers, it compiles existing WHO recommendations and evidence to support the planning, implementation and scale-up of integrated, people-centred sexual health services. The document outlines the epidemiology and burden of STIs, particularly among populations who may benefit from or use PrEP, and highlights the public health rationale for strengthening STI prevention, testing, treatment and follow-up within PrEP delivery platforms.

The module describes practical approaches to integrating STI services across different service delivery models, including considerations related to workforce capacity, task sharing, monitoring, financing and demand generation. It presents guidance on counselling, health promotion, screening, diagnostic testing, partner services, clinical management, referral pathways and prevention measures such as condom provision and vaccination. Emphasizing differentiated service delivery and human rights principles, the publication aims to improve access to comprehensive sexual health care, enhance service quality and support efforts to reduce the burden of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections through coordinated and efficient health-system responses.

title: WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis: module 5: management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents
abstract:
This operational handbook provides practical guidance for implementing World Health Organization recommendations on the prevention, screening, diagnosis and management of tuberculosis (TB) in children and adolescents under programmatic conditions and across different levels of the health system. Developed alongside the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, the publication addresses the specific epidemiological, clinical and psychosocial vulnerabilities of children and adolescents affected by TB, including challenges related to diagnosis, treatment adherence, prevention and continuity of care. The handbook aims to support the development and revision of national policies, operational guidance and service delivery approaches tailored to the needs of these populations.

The handbook covers the full continuum of TB care, including contact investigation, systematic screening, preventive treatment, diagnostic approaches for pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB, and treatment of drug-susceptible and drug-resistant disease. It also addresses decentralized and family-centred models of care, management of TB in children and adolescents living with HIV, TB during pregnancy, malnutrition, pneumonia, adolescent health needs and palliative care. Practical tools, implementation guidance and standard operating procedures are included to support programme managers and health-care providers in strengthening child and adolescent TB services.

title: Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health
abstract:
This second edition of the Classification of Digital Interventions, Services and Applications in Health provides a standardized taxonomy for describing how digital technologies are used to address individual and health system needs. Developed by WHO, the classification establishes a shared language to support communication among policy-makers, health programme managers, researchers, implementers, technology developers and other stakeholders involved in digital health. It organizes digital health interventions around discrete technological capabilities designed to address health system challenges and links these interventions to the digital services and application types through which they are delivered.

The publication updates and expands the first edition published in 2018 to reflect advances in digital health technologies, evolving implementation practices and lessons learned from global use. The framework is structured around three interconnected axes: health system challenges, digital health interventions and digital services and application types. It includes interventions for persons, health-care providers, health system managers and data services, alongside categories of digital applications and information systems. The classification is intended to support planning, implementation, investment analysis, research, interoperability considerations, policy development and the governance of digital health initiatives, thereby facilitating more consistent and effective use of digital technologies in health systems.

title: Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems
abstract:
This second edition of the digital adaptation kit for HIV provides operational, software-neutral requirements to support the incorporation of WHO clinical, public health and data use recommendations into digital systems. Developed within the SMART Guidelines approach, it focuses on the content requirements for person-centred digital tracking and decision support systems used by health workers for HIV services in primary health care settings. The kit is intended to facilitate transparent, consistent and adaptable translation of narrative guidance into digital implementations while supporting interoperability and local customization.

The publication organizes HIV-related requirements into eight components: health interventions and associated recommendations; generic personas; illustrative user scenarios; business processes and workflows; core data elements; decision support and scheduling logic; indicators and performance metrics; and high-level functional and non-functional requirements. It covers processes including HIV testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis, care and treatment, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, infant diagnosis, diagnostics, client follow-up, referral, and aggregate reporting and data use, with complementary operational resources provided in web annexes.

title: Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing: WHO recommendations in digital systems: web annex A: data dictionary
abstract: This web annex provides the standardized data dictionary supporting the WHO Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. It defines the core data elements required to implement WHO recommendations across HIV prevention, testing, treatment, care, diagnostics, referral, follow-up and reporting workflows in digital health systems. The annex specifies standardized data element names, definitions, data types, permissible values, calculated fields, coding structures and unique identifiers to support consistent data capture, interoperability and alignment with international terminology standards. Organized according to the business processes described in the digital adaptation kit, it also includes guidance on adapting the data dictionary to national programme requirements while preserving standardized information exchange. Intended for digital health architects, software developers, implementers and programme managers, this resource provides a practical foundation for configuring, customizing and maintaining interoperable HIV information systems that accurately reflect WHO recommendations.

title: Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing: WHO recommendations in digital systems: web annex B: decision-support logic
abstract: This web annex provides the standardized decision-support logic supporting the WHO Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. It translates WHO HIV recommendations into structured, software-neutral decision tables that can be incorporated into digital tracking and decision-support systems to support consistent clinical and public health decision-making. The annex includes decision logic for HIV testing, prevention, treatment, advanced HIV disease, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, diagnostics, follow-up and related service delivery workflows, using standardized input expressions, decision rules, outputs, scheduling logic and triggering events. It also provides implementation guidance on rule syntax, comparison operators, hit policies and coding conventions to promote transparency, interoperability and consistent interpretation across digital platforms. Intended for software developers, digital health architects, implementers and programme managers, this resource supports the development and adaptation of standards-based decision-support functionality that accurately reflects WHO recommendations while allowing contextualization for national policies and health system requirements.

title: Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing: WHO recommendations in digital systems: web annex C: indicators table
abstract: This web annex provides the standardized indicators and performance metrics supporting the WHO Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. It defines a comprehensive set of indicators for monitoring HIV prevention, testing, treatment, care, diagnostics and programme performance, translating WHO recommendations into standardized indicator specifications that can be incorporated into digital health systems. For each indicator, the annex documents indicator definitions, calculation methods, numerators and denominators, disaggregation variables, required data elements, reporting requirements, data sources, implementation notes and mappings to international monitoring frameworks, including WHO, UNAIDS, Global Fund and PEPFAR indicators where applicable. Intended for programme managers, monitoring and evaluation specialists, digital health architects and software developers, this resource supports the standardized measurement, reporting and analysis of HIV programme performance while promoting interoperability, consistent implementation of WHO recommendations and adaptation to national monitoring requirements.

title: Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing: WHO recommendations in digital systems: web annex D: function and non-functional requirements
abstract: This web annex provides the high-level functional and non-functional requirements supporting the WHO Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. It translates WHO HIV recommendations and service delivery workflows into standardized system requirements to guide the design, development, procurement and implementation of interoperable digital health solutions. The annex defines functional requirements for key business processes across HIV prevention, testing, treatment, care, diagnostics, referral, follow-up and reporting, together with non-functional requirements addressing system performance, security, confidentiality, privacy, interoperability, usability, reliability and offline functionality. Structured as a software-neutral implementation resource, it enables consistent interpretation of operational requirements while allowing adaptation to national policies and digital health architectures. Intended for digital health architects, software developers, implementers, procurers and programme managers, this resource supports the development of standards-based HIV information systems that accurately implement WHO recommendations while ensuring robust, secure and sustainable digital health solutions.

title: National health workforce accounts: a handbook
abstract:
The National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) Handbook, second edition, provides the conceptual framework, standards, methods and indicators that support the systematic collection, analysis and use of health workforce data for evidence-informed policy-making and planning. Developed by the World Health Organization, the handbook supports implementation of the National Health Workforce Accounts as a country-led system to strengthen human resources for health information systems, improve data quality and availability, and monitor progress towards universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals and other global health objectives. It describes the rationale, principles and applications of NHWA at national, regional and global levels and outlines a modular approach to health workforce monitoring.

The handbook presents guidance on implementation and reporting methods and defines a set of standardized indicators organized into four modules covering workforce stock and flows, education, finance and expenditures, and working conditions, governance and leadership. It explains indicator metadata, calculation methods, disaggregation requirements and reporting standards, and illustrates how NHWA data can be used to support workforce planning, policy development, retention strategies, equity analyses and monitoring of health workforce trends. The revised edition incorporates updated indicators, occupational classifications, tools and guidance to address evolving health workforce priorities and emerging global health challenges.

title: Pandemic influenza preparedness framework: annual progress report, 1 January – 31 December 2022
abstract:
The Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Framework: annual progress report, 1 January–31 December 2022 presents technical and financial progress in implementing the PIP Framework, which aims to strengthen the sharing of influenza viruses with human pandemic potential and improve developing countries’ access to pandemic vaccines and other response supplies. The report assesses progress under the High-Level Implementation Plan II (2018–2023), including activities financed through the industry-funded Partnership Contribution mechanism.

The report documents achievements and challenges in influenza laboratory capacity and surveillance, virus sharing, disease burden estimation, regulatory preparedness, risk communication and community engagement, deployment planning, and national pandemic preparedness. In 2022, 91% of Partnership Contribution recipient countries reported influenza data to FluNet, 48 countries had implemented regulatory approaches for pandemic influenza products, and 37 countries had developed or updated pandemic preparedness plans. It also presents progress in securing pandemic response products through benefit-sharing agreements, alongside financial allocations, expenditures and implementation milestones.

title: Poliovirus containment: guidance to minimize risk for facilities collecting, handling or storing materials potentially infectious for polioviruses: web annex A: country and area specific poliovirus data, April 2023 update
abstract:
This web annex provides updated country- and area-specific poliovirus circulation data to support the assessment of potentially infectious materials in facilities collecting, handling or storing samples that may contain polioviruses. It accompanies the second edition of Poliovirus containment: guidance to minimize risks for facilities collecting, handling or storing materials potentially infectious for polioviruses and is intended to assist facilities in identifying samples requiring appropriate risk mitigation or containment measures.

The annex presents Table A2.1, which compiles poliovirus circulation dates by country and area, including wild poliovirus (WPV), vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) and oral polio vaccine type 2/novel oral polio vaccine type 2/Sabin2 potentially infectious material periods. The data were derived from national poliovirus reports, systematic literature searches and consultations with WHO regional offices, and are regularly revised and updated. The information supports the identification and management of potentially infectious materials according to the containment requirements outlined in the accompanying guidance.

title: Toolkit for analysis and use of routine health facility data: integrated health services analysis: district and facility level
abstract:
This guidance document, part of the WHO Toolkit for analysis and use of routine health facility data, provides practical guidance on the integrated analysis and use of routine health information system (RHIS) data at district and health facility levels. It is intended to support managers, analysts and other health system stakeholders in monitoring health service delivery and using routine data for operational decision-making. The document promotes an integrated, standards-based approach that uses a limited set of tracer indicators representing multiple programmes and service components, thereby supporting primary health care, universal health coverage and the health-related Sustainable Development Goals.

The publication presents principles for RHIS data analysis, including integration across programmes, focused use of key indicators, standardization of analyses and visualizations, routine assessment of data quality, and purpose-oriented use of information for management and planning. It organizes indicators into three groups: health status and epidemiological profile, health service performance, and health service resources. For each group, the publication provides indicator definitions, metadata, recommended disaggregations, analytical approaches, and examples of dashboards and visualizations. It emphasizes the interpretation of routine data within local contexts and illustrates how standardized dashboards can support supervision, performance review, resource allocation and continuous improvement of health services at subnational levels.

title: Digital adaptation kit for immunizations: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems
abstract:
This publication presents the World Health Organization’s digital adaptation kit (DAK) for immunizations, developed within the SMART Guidelines framework to support the implementation of WHO immunization recommendations in digital systems. The document provides operational and software-neutral specifications intended to facilitate the translation of immunization guidance into interoperable digital health applications, particularly person-centred point-of-service systems and electronic immunization registries. It outlines the role of digital adaptation kits in strengthening digital health systems by improving the consistency, transparency and standardization of health content, workflows, data structures and decision-support logic used in immunization programmes. The publication also situates the DAK within broader digital health strategies and interoperability standards.

The document describes eight core components of the immunization DAK, including health interventions and recommendations, generic personas, user scenarios, workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, indicators and functional requirements. It incorporates WHO guidance related to routine immunization, electronic immunization registries and digital health interventions, while emphasizing adaptability to country-specific policies and implementation contexts. Additional sections address interoperability, data standards, workflow optimization and the use of digital systems to support longitudinal tracking, reporting, decision support and communication within immunization services. The publication is intended for immunization programme managers, digital health teams, software developers and implementers involved in designing and deploying digital immunization systems.

title: Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture
abstract:
This handbook provides practical guidance for countries seeking to digitally transform public health supply chains through the development of coherent strategies, interoperable architectures and sustainable implementation approaches. Developed within the WHO SMART Guidelines framework, it addresses the growing need for integrated digital ecosystems that support forecasting, procurement, warehousing, distribution, dispensing and traceability of health products. The publication outlines the role of digital technologies in improving efficiency, data availability, interoperability and decision-making across supply chain processes, while helping ensure timely access to quality-assured medicines and health products.

The publication presents a stepwise approach for defining a digital health supply chain (DHSC) strategy, assessing existing health supply chain information systems, designing a target architecture, planning implementation and supporting product traceability. It emphasizes stakeholder engagement, alignment with national health, digital health and supply chain strategies, use of open standards, and long-term scalability and sustainability. Drawing on country experiences and established digital health frameworks, the handbook offers practical tools, templates and examples to support governance, planning and coordination of digital transformation initiatives, with the aim of strengthening supply chain performance, improving visibility across the supply chain and enhancing patient safety.

title: Digital transformation handbook for primary health care: optimizing person-centred point of service systems
abstract:
This handbook provides practical guidance for countries seeking to digitally transform primary health care through the development and implementation of person-centred point of service systems (PCPOSS). It addresses the transition from paper-based and fragmented digital systems towards integrated, interoperable digital solutions that support service delivery, continuity of care, data use and health system strengthening. Grounded in WHO recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening and aligned with the SMART Guidelines framework, the publication outlines approaches for translating clinical and public health guidance into digital systems while maintaining fidelity to normative standards.

The publication presents a stepwise methodology covering assessment of digital readiness, identification of user requirements, workflow and business process mapping, system design and adaptation, software selection, testing, deployment and scale-up. It emphasizes person-centred care, interoperability, longitudinal health records, decision support and the use of standards-based digital architectures. Through practical tools, worksheets and implementation guidance, the publication supports policy-makers, programme managers, digital health practitioners and software developers in designing and optimizing digital systems that improve service quality, strengthen accountability and enable more effective, integrated and responsive primary health care services.

title: Digital transformation handbook for health product catalogue
abstract:
This handbook provides guidance for the implementation of standardized product master data management through national product catalogues (NPCs) to support digital transformation in health supply chains. Developed within the framework of the WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide and aligned with the SMART Guidelines initiative, the publication outlines regulatory, governance, technological and operational approaches for establishing interoperable product registries and harmonized product information systems. It explains the importance of standardized product master data for ensuring accurate identification, tracking and management of health products across manufacturers, regulatory authorities, procurement entities, warehouses, health facilities and other supply chain stakeholders.

The handbook describes policies and procedures for data governance, coding structures, interoperability standards, change management and capacity-building to support sustainable implementation. It also presents guidance on integrating standardized product master data with digital health, regulatory and supply chain systems to improve forecasting, procurement, inventory management, pharmacovigilance, product recalls and traceability. In addition, the publication highlights mechanisms for sharing product master data as a global good and leveraging WHO-hosted tools and open standards to strengthen coordination, data quality and supply chain efficiency across countries and organizations.

title: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis
abstract:
This web annex to the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 3: Diagnosis, compiles the evidence synthesis and analyses used to inform WHO recommendations on diagnostic technologies for tuberculosis and drug-resistant tuberculosis. The publication presents systematic reviews, meta-analyses, qualitative evidence syntheses and economic evaluations examining the diagnostic accuracy, safety, cost–effectiveness and implementation considerations of multiple diagnostic approaches, including low- and moderate-complexity nucleic acid amplification tests, targeted next-generation sequencing technologies and Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests.

The annex describes the methods applied to identify, assess and synthesize evidence across diverse populations and settings, including adults, adolescents, children and people living with HIV. It addresses the detection of pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis, rifampicin resistance and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis using respiratory and non-respiratory specimens. The document also examines stakeholder and user perspectives, operational feasibility and factors influencing implementation. Developed in accordance with WHO guideline development standards, the annex provides the technical evidence base underpinning updates to WHO policy guidance on tuberculosis diagnosis and drug-resistance testing.

title: Consolidated HIV guidelines: service delivery
abstract:
HIV remains a major public health challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, despite the availability of effective treatment and prevention tools. Many evidence-based interventions are not implemented consistently or delivered in a timely manner, contributing to ongoing HIV transmission, advanced disease and preventable mortality. These consolidated WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations to strengthen HIV service delivery through people-centred, integrated and equitable approaches that improve access to care, continuity of treatment and accelerate progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat.

The publication consolidates all WHO recommendations on HIV service delivery issued between 2013 and 2025. It is intended to support the development of national and subnational policies, clinical guidelines and implementation guidance. It addresses key components of HIV service delivery, including linkage to care and antiretroviral therapy initiation, clinical follow-up and medication refills, adherence support and re-engagement in care, services for adolescents and young people, task sharing, decentralized service delivery, and integration with maternal and child health, tuberculosis, sexual and reproductive health, diabetes, hypertension and mental health services. Recommendations are classified as new, updated or revalidated according to WHO guideline development procedures.

title: Digital transformation handbook for reporting substandard and falsified medical products
abstract:
This handbook provides practical guidance to support countries in planning, designing and implementing digital solutions for reporting substandard and falsified medical products. These products pose a significant threat to public health, contributing to therapeutic failure, adverse effects, loss of trust in health systems and broader socioeconomic impacts. Effective detection and reporting are essential to enable regulatory authorities to investigate suspected cases, remove harmful products from circulation and contribute to global surveillance efforts through mechanisms such as WHO’s Global Surveillance and Monitoring System.

The document outlines a structured approach to digital transformation, covering assessment of the current environment, stakeholder engagement, governance and policy alignment, definition of system requirements, implementation planning, and monitoring and evaluation. It emphasizes the transition from fragmented or paper-based reporting systems to interoperable digital platforms that improve data quality, standardization and timeliness. Drawing on global experience and existing WHO frameworks, the handbook promotes the use of user-centred design, open standards and integration with pharmacovigilance systems. It is intended for ministries of health, national regulatory authorities and partners seeking to strengthen reporting systems and enhance the capacity to detect and respond to substandard and falsified medical products.

title: Global hepatitis report 2026
abstract:
This report provides a comprehensive assessment of the global burden of viral hepatitis and progress towards the goal of eliminating hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. Drawing on data reported by Member States and modelled estimates, it analyses trends in incidence, prevalence and mortality associated with hepatitis B and C, covering the period from 2015 to 2024 based on the latest available data. It also situates these trends within the context of global commitments, strategies and targets.

The publication reviews the coverage and impact of key interventions for prevention, diagnosis and treatment, including vaccination, infection prevention and control, harm reduction and access to antiviral therapies. It identifies persistent gaps in testing and treatment, marked regional disparities, and the need for accelerated scale-up of services, particularly in high-burden settings. The report concludes that progress towards the 2030 elimination targets remains off track despite the availability of effective interventions. Intended for policymakers, programme managers and public health stakeholders, it serves as an analytical and strategic resource to guide national and global responses to viral hepatitis.

title: National health workforce accounts: health workforce levels and trends 2026
abstract:
This report presents the 2026 edition of the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) series, providing an overview of the status of NHWA implementation and an analysis of global and regional health workforce levels and trends based on official data reported by countries to the World Health Organization. Developed to support evidence-informed health workforce policy-making and planning, the report examines progress in strengthening national health workforce information systems, data availability and reporting across countries, and the use of standardized indicators to monitor human resources for health in support of universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals and other health objectives.

Drawing on the 2025 NHWA data release, the report analyses the distribution, density and composition of the health and care workforce across regions and income groups, highlighting persistent disparities in workforce availability. It also examines trends in workforce growth since 2006 and presents a thematic analysis of population ageing and health workforce ageing, assessing their implications for future workforce needs. The findings demonstrate substantial improvements in the availability and quality of health workforce data through NHWA implementation while underscoring continuing challenges related to workforce shortages, inequities in distribution and the need for sustained investment in health workforce planning and monitoring.

title: Guidelines for the prevention and control of infection with LAV/HTLV III

author.literal: World Health Organization. Control Programme on AIDS

abstract:
These guidelines provide recommendations for preventing and controlling infection with LAV/HTLV-III, the retrovirus recognized at the time as the etiological agent of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Developed as part of the WHO AIDS Control Programme, they are intended primarily for public health authorities and health professionals, who are responsible for adapting the guidance to different populations and settings. The document summarizes available knowledge on transmission, clinical manifestations, laboratory detection, surveillance, notification and confidentiality, and case definitions for AIDS.

The guidelines emphasize routine precautions to prevent exposure to blood and other potentially infectious body fluids, particularly among health care workers, laboratory personnel and providers of home and emergency care. They address prevention and management of needlestick, parenteral and mucous-membrane exposures, safe handling of specimens and contaminated equipment, and precautions for non-health-care workers. Guidance is also provided on disinfection, sterilization, and the safe processing of reusable needles, syringes and other instruments.

title: 8th National Tuberculosis Programme Managers Meeting and 13th Wolfheze Workshop: Wolfheze 2008: tuberculosis management, surveillance and evaluation in Europe with high rates or threat of multidrug resistant tuberculosis: The Hague, the Netherlands, 1–2 June 2008

author.literal: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe

publisher: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe
abstract: The WHO European Region has the highest rates in the world of drug-resistant tuberculosis and increasing rates of HIV/tuberculosis coinfection. Eighteen high-priority countries have been identified to urgently scale up tuberculosis control interventions: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Bulgaria, Estonia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia, Lithuania, the Republic of Moldova, Romania, the Russian Federation, Tajikistan, Turkey, Turkmenistan, Ukraine and Uzbekistan. Five of these countries are members of the European Union. Migration and pockets of poverty increase vulnerability to tuberculosis in many western European countries. Related areas, such as the rapid detection of drug-resistant tuberculosis, contact tracing, infection control, health system strengthening and the review of national tuberculosis programmes, are of equal concern among eastern, central and western countries of the WHO European Region. While general awareness and political commitment were raised during the Ministerial Forum held in Berlin in October 2007, how to ensure the follow-up of the Berlin Declaration on TB and monitor its implementation is currently under discussion. The 8th National Tuberculosis Programme Managers Meeting and the 13th Wolfheze Workshop, jointly organized in June 2008 in The Hague, provided a forum for discussion on each of the aforementioned topics and facilitated the sharing of experiences between countries in the Region – which are very different from an epidemiological, organizational, cultural and wealth perspective.

title: The case for investing in public health: the strengthening public health services and capacity. A key pillar of the European regional health policy framework Health 2020

author.literal: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe

publisher: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe
abstract: The economic crisis has led to increased demand and reduced resources for health sectors. The trend for increasing healthcare costs to individuals, the health sector and wider society is significant. Public health can be part of the solution to this challenge. The evidence shows that prevention can be cost-effective, provide value for money andgive returns on investment in both the short and longer terms. This public health summary outlines quick returns on investment for health and other sectors for interventions that promote physical activity and healthy employment; address housing and mental health; and reduce road traffic injuries and violence. Vaccinations and screening programmes are largely cost-effective. Population-level approaches are estimated to cost on average five times less than individual interventions. This report gives examples of interventions with early returns on investment and approaches with longer-term gains. Investing in cost-effective interventions to reduce costs to the health sector and other sectors can help create sustainable health systems and economies for the future.

title: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006

author.literal: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia

publisher: WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia
abstract: Description: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes is essential for initiation of antiretroviral therapy for a person with HIV as well as for monitoring the response to treatment. The techniques for enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes are evolving. The flow cytometry continues to be the gold standard of CD4 T lymphocytes enumeration in spite of the fact that the technology is expensive both in terms of initial investment in sophisticated equipment and running cost. The newer techniques may be economical to procure and maintain. The latter are particularly intended for countries with limited resources. WHO conducted a workshop to orient the nationals about these technologies and integration of a quality system into routine testing, at Siriraj Hospital Bangkok. The report describes the status of CD4 testing in these countries. While Indonesia, India and Thailand have developed a good infrastructure for enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal and Sri Lanka have made a beginning in this direction. The workshop focussed on principles of various techniques and imparted a hands-on training for performing the same. The issues regarding selection of technology, procurement of equipment and their maintenance; ensuring continuous supply and economical use of reagents and biosafety in laboratory were discussed and have been presented in this Report.

تصنيف التدخلات والخدمات والتطبيقات الرقمية في مجال الصحة: لغة مشتركة لوصف استخدامات التكنولوجيا الرقمية من أجل الصحة
abstract:
تقدم هذه الطبعة الثانية من «تصنيف التدخلات والخدمات والتطبيقات الرقمية في مجال الصحة» تصنيفاً معيارياً يصف كيفية استخدام التقنيات الرقمية لتلبية احتياجات الأفراد والنظم الصحية. وقد أعدت منظمة الصحة العالمية هذا التصنيف ليكون لغة مشتركة تدعم التواصل بين صانعي السياسات، ومديري البرامج الصحية، والباحثين، والمنفذين، ومطوري التكنولوجيا، وغيرهم من أصحاب المصلحة في مجال الصحة الرقمية. وينظم التصنيف التدخلات الصحية الرقمية حول قدرات تكنولوجية محددة صُممت لمعالجة التحديات التي تواجه النظم الصحية، ويربط هذه التدخلات بالخدمات وأنواع التطبيقات الرقمية التي تُستخدم لتنفيذها.

ويُحدِّث هذا المنشور ويوسِّع الطبعة الأولى الصادرة عام 2018 ليعكس التقدم في تقنيات الصحة الرقمية، وتطور ممارسات التنفيذ، والدروس المستفادة من استخدامها على المستوى العالمي. ويستند الإطار إلى ثلاثة محاور مترابطة: تحديات النظم الصحية، والتدخلات الصحية الرقمية، والخدمات وأنواع التطبيقات الرقمية. ويشمل تدخلات موجهة للأفراد، ولمقدمي الرعاية الصحية، ولمديري النظم الصحية، ولخدمات البيانات، إلى جانب فئات التطبيقات الرقمية ونظم المعلومات. ويهدف هذا التصنيف إلى دعم التخطيط والتنفيذ، وتحليل الاستثمارات، والبحوث، واعتبارات التشغيل البيني، وصياغة السياسات، وحوكمة مبادرات الصحة الرقمية، بما يعزز الاستخدام المنسق والفعال للتقنيات الرقمية في النظم الصحية.
